obtained.how: the publisher's typeset article (TAFS 139: 353–361) as once posted openly on the Illinois Natural History Survey stream-ecology lab website (INHS is the authors' institution); the live link now returns 404, so it was read from the Wayback Machine's capture of 28 May 2024 (openly downloadable, no login). The INHS file carries a ResearchGate cover page (saying co-author D. E. Shoup uploaded it there in May 2014); nothing was fetched from ResearchGate itself

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the title page (Transactions of the American Fisheries Society 139:353–361, 2010; DOI 10.1577/T08-159.1; published online 31 December 2009)
bibliography.note: issue 2 is Crossref's; the title page gives volume and pages only

claims.claim: adult smallmouth offered crayfish, golden shiner and round goby avoided crayfish or showed no preference for them in every treatment (Carter et al. 2010; abstract only)
claims.location: p. 353 (PDF p. 2), abstract; p. 356 (PDF p. 5), results and Fig. 1
claims.quote: crayfish were negatively or neutrally selected in all trials across both turbidity and cover
claims.conditions: laboratory: 15 smallmouth 230–355 mm TL (mean 290), each tested once in each of 10 treatments (0, 5, 10, 20, 40 NTU × cover or none; 148 trials) in 1,600-L tanks at 18–19 °C after 24 h without food; five each of northern crayfish (44 mm TL), golden shiner (70 mm) and round goby (68 mm), sizes chosen as each prey's 'optimal' size; a trial ended once 1–4 prey were eaten; selection by Chesson's alpha against 1/3
claims.note: full text read: drop '(abstract only)'. In clear water without cover the bass selected round goby; with cover, golden shiners

claims.claim: bass do not prefer crayfish when fish are available
claims.quote: smallmouth bass do not prefer crayfish more than other prey types
claims.conditions: the authors' reading of their trials together with Kim (2007; round goby, emerald shiner and crayfish offered: crayfish eaten least); they add that crayfish may be the commonest prey where smallmouth live, which explains the field diets

claims.claim: given fish, smallmouth avoid crayfish or take them at chance (Carter et al. 2010)
claims.quote: Northern crayfish were negatively or neutrally selected in all trials
claims.conditions: as in the first claim ('neutral' = the 95 % CI of Chesson's alpha overlaps random feeding, 1/3)

tried.note: the live INHS copy is gone; its Wayback capture was used

notes: Useful beyond the cited sentence (pp. 356–358): prey eaten per hour fell with turbidity (highest at 0 NTU; r = −0.3) and did not differ with cover; Secchi depth 62.5, 45.8, 33.5 and 24.5 cm at 5, 10, 20 and 40 NTU; energy densities quoted: crayfish 3.12 kJ/g wet (Kelso 1973), round goby 3.65 (Kim 2007), emerald shiner 5.14 (Bryan et al. 1996). The authors call smallmouth 'generalist predators' whose field diets reflect encounter rates rather than preference — a direct support for the code's CR_PREF reasoning. Caveat for the rewrite: short laboratory trials with 'optimal'-sized prey at a fixed density (5.9 fish/m²), with bass that had been fed all three prey beforehand.
